description: A fixture of the aviation world since it launched in the 1920s, Delta is one of the world’s largest airlines by passengers and by revenue. It has numerous U.S. hub cities, the biggest of which is Atlanta, where Delta is headquartered. The airline’s routes span most of the world, including Asia and Latin America. Delta’s iconic red triangle logo is suggestive of flight and the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet. The airline also helped popularize Biscoff cookies—the name a portmanteau of biscuit and coffee—as an in-flight snack.

title: Delta Air Lines

rankings.title: 100 Best Large Workplaces for Women
rankings.itemDescription:
Employees say:

"Delta goes through changes every single day, but one thing remains constant—you’re never left behind. We’re fortunate to have leaders who guide and support us through it all. They encourage us to grow, challenge us to be the best version of ourselves, and genuinely care. What I truly appreciate is how approachable they are. Even when we simply wave or say hello, they acknowledge us with warmth and sincerity. I’m grateful for our leaders and team leads—for their presence, their support, and the way they make a difference every day."

rankings.title: Best Workplaces in Transportation
rankings.itemDescription:
Employees say:

"In 2018 my spouse was diagnosed with cancer and both my company and team members stepped up in many ways to support during that unexpected time of need. My company not only provided me an expected period paid of leave, they also extended me the courtesy of working remotely as I attended to her throughout her treatments, multiple surgeries and the (unforeseen) extended period of recovery and home care that occurred over a 18 month period. The many acts of kindness, professionalism and genuine caring demonstrated by both my company and teammates is what makes this Delta Air Lines a great place to work."

rankings.title: Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For
rankings.itemDescription:
Delta Air Lines handed out $1.3 billion in bonuses this year to its more than 100,000 workers worldwide after posting strong earnings, bringing total employee profit-sharing to $11 billion since 2015. Staffers also get unlimited standby travel privileges to any destination Delta serves, along with discounts on tickets and vacation packages.

Employees say:

"I truly appreciate how Delta listens to employee feedback and continues to innovate in ways that drive meaningful improvement. What I love most is that we are recognized not just as employees, but as family. The sense of community here is incredibly strong, and the diversity within our teams is something I find truly beautiful. Delta has been a part of my life since birth, thanks to my father also being a member of this incredible team since 2005. For us, Delta is more than a company - it's generational, and it's home."

rankings.title: 100 Best Large Workplaces for Women
rankings.itemDescription:
Employees say:

"I absolutely love working for this company and the family dynamic that it has. I love how inclusive the executives are and how they make us (the regular ground workers and hourly workers) feel important by including us in all of the big decisions Delta makes. For an example within the first year of joining Delta I was able to meet the CEO of the company, and I was able to ask him different questions directly about the future of Delta and listen to him speak. I've never been with a company that has made me feel so important and like my voice matters until I started working with Delta."

rankings.title: Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For
rankings.itemDescription: Employees say: "Delta provides an amazing place to develop a career, not just a job. People care for each other here and push each other to be better every day. When an employee hits a personal or family challenge, the company steps up and does right by them. My family experienced a medical issue, and the support and care that Delta provided to help us deal with the medical issue went above and beyond what was required or normal."

rankings.title: Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For
rankings.itemDescription: Delta Air Lines employs over 100,000 people and services more than 4,000 daily flights to hundreds of destinations on six continents. With over 200 million annual customers, the airline company values its employees by raising pay, eliminating college-degree requirements, and instilling antiracism action plans. In April of last year, Delta increased the base pay for its operations employees by a flat 5%, and reported an average 5% increase for its salaried employees worldwide. It also offers a Shared Rewards program for its employees to earn 10% of corporate profits from their first dollar earned, through which employees earned a total of $61 million in 2022. Last February, Delta announced a profit-sharing payment of $1,250 to every eligible employee and later extended its payments through a 4% base pay raise in May, followed by another base pay increase of 5% in April. Delta also partners with Care.com to give workers last-minute care for children, adults, and pets with rates as low as $6 an hour.

rankings.title: Fortune 500
rankings.itemDescription:
The Atlanta-based carrier moved 28 spots up this year’s list, thanks to a robust travel rebound in the wake of the COVID-era slowdown. Its operating revenue for the year reached $50.6 billion, up 69% from 2021.

  • In May 2022, Delta said it would remove 100 flights a day from its summer schedule to stave off travel chaos as it rebuilt its operations. In the month to follow, however, CEO Ed Bastian apologized for delays and the disruption of hundreds of flights owing in part to understaffing.

  • Delta reached a deal with its pilots’ union in March 2023 to boost pay by 34% over three years.

  • Inflation threatened Delta’s profits in early 2023, but the company anticipates a 2% to 4% nonfuel unit cost decline through the year compared with 2022.

  • Still, Delta faces a pilot shortage and the delayed delivery of new aircraft, which could reduce flight volume and raise airfares.

  • The airline expects flight demand to grow in 2023, which will help offset higher expenses, like the surging cost of fuel and labor.

Fortune 500
rankings.itemDescription: The Atlanta-based airline was heavily challenged in 2020 as air travel was all but grounded during the pandemic. Its revenue fell 64% to $17.1 billion and it lost more than $12 billion. This year, the carrier has so far reported $4 million in daily cash generation in March, an improvement from the $11 million daily cash burn on average for the quarter ended in March 2021.

rankings.title: Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For
Fortune Global 500
rankings.itemDescription: In retrospect, 2019 was a halcyon year for the travel industry. Fuel was cheap, travel demand was high, and as the only major U.S. airline without Boeing 737 MAX planes in its fleet, Delta sidestepped the fallout from their grounding. Annual revenue rose 5.8% to $47 billion, and net income jumped 21.1% to $4.8 billion, giving Delta its tenth straight year of profitability—if likely the last it will see for some time. After the pandemic closed down most airline travel and led Delta and its competitors to seek government aid, CEO Ed Bastian predicted that Delta will need at least three years to get back to a sustainable—but still sub-2019—level of travel. As Bastian told Fortune: “This is going to take a long time.”

rankings.title: Fortune 500
rankings.itemDescription: In retrospect, 2019 was a halcyon year for the travel industry and especially for Delta, which climbed past American to claim the title of the largest airline on the Fortune 500. Fuel was cheap, travel demand was high, and as the only major U.S. airline without Boeing 737 MAX planes in its fleet, Delta sidestepped the fallout from their grounding. Annual revenue rose 5.8% to $47 billion, and net income jumped 21.1% to $4.8 billion, giving Delta its tenth straight year of profitability—if likely the last it will see for some time. After the pandemic closed down most airline travel and led Delta and its competitors to seek government aid, CEO Ed Bastian predicted that Delta will need at least three years to get back to a sustainable—but still sub-2019—level of travel. As CEO Ed Bastian told Fortune: “This is going to take a long time.”
